#1
L: Supreme, again I shall declare — of-knowledges the knowledge, best — having known which, all sages have gone hence to supreme perfection.
I: I shall speak once more of the supreme knowledge, the best among knowledges, by knowing which all the sages have attained the highest perfection.
N: This chapter opens with no question from Arjuna; Kṛṣṇa simply continues speaking, and bhūyaḥ, 'again, further', signals that what follows continues and completes the teaching on prakṛti and puruṣa begun in chapter 13. Jñānānāṃ jñānam uttamam, 'the best knowledge among knowledges' (a partitive genitive), anticipates the doctrine of the three guṇas that occupies the rest of the chapter, and para, 'supreme', already used of brahman at 13.17, is here applied to this teaching itself. Sandhi: yajjñātvā is yat+jñātvā (-t+j-→-j j-); siddhim ito packs siddhim+itaḥ (simply joined, -m unaffected before the vowel) and itaḥ+gatāḥ (-aḥ before g-→-o).
#2
L: This knowledge having relied upon, [they] have come to my same-nature; at creation too they are not born, and at dissolution they are not disturbed.
I: Relying on this knowledge, they have come to share my own nature; they are not born even at a new creation, nor are they troubled at its dissolution.
N: Sādharmya, 'sameness of nature/dharma [with me]', names the goal already promised in these very terms at 13.18's mad-bhāvāya: those who grasp this knowledge cease to be swept up in the endless cycle of sarga and pralaya, 'creation' and 'dissolution', that governs ordinary souls born again at every new world-age. Sandhi: sarge'pi is sarge+api (-e+a-→-e' with avagraha); nopajāyante is na+upajāyante (-a+u-→-o-).
#3
L: My womb [is] the-great-brahman; in that I place the-germ. The-origination of-all-beings comes from-that, O Bhārata.
I: The great brahman is my womb; in it I place the seed. From that, Bhārata, comes the coming-into-being of every creature.
N: This opens a brief cosmogony (continued at verse 4): mahad brahma, 'the great brahman' — here primordial, unevolved nature (prakṛti), not the transcendent brahman described at 13.12-17 — receives Kṛṣṇa's garbham, 'germ, seed', the act of insemination from which all beings arise. Sandhi: yonir mahad brahma packs yoniḥ+mahat (-iḥ+m-→-ir m-) and mahat+brahma (-t+b-→-d b-); dadhāmy ahaṃ is dadhāmi+aham (-i+a-→-y a-).
#4
L: In-all-wombs, O Kaunteya, whatever forms arise — of-them, brahman [is] the-great-womb; I [am] the-seed-giving father.
I: Whatever forms come to be in any womb, Kaunteya, brahman is their great womb, and I am the father who supplies the seed.
N: This completes the cosmogony of verse 3: every mūrti, 'form, embodiment', born in any yoni, 'womb' (any species, any realm), has mahad brahma for its universal matrix, with Kṛṣṇa as bīja-pradaḥ pitā, 'the seed-giving father' — the same pairing of matter as womb and spirit as begetter that verses 5 onward recast as the guṇas of prakṛti binding the puruṣa. Sandhi: mahadyonir ahaṃ packs mahat+yoniḥ (-t+y-→-d y-) and yoniḥ+aham (-iḥ+a-→-ir a-).
#5
L: Sattva, rajas, tamas — thus [named], the-guṇas, born-of-nature, bind, O mighty-armed one, in-the-body the-imperishable embodied-one.
I: Sattva, rajas, and tamas — these are the guṇas that arise from nature; they bind the imperishable soul, mighty-armed one, within the body.
N: This opens the chapter's central teaching, naming all three guṇas together for the first time in the poem (individual guṇas were named earlier, e.g. 7.12-13, but not defined until here) and stating at once their basic effect: to nibadhnanti, 'bind', the dehin, the otherwise avyaya, 'imperishable', embodied self, within the deha, 'body'. Verses 6-8 define each guṇa in turn; verses 9-13 describe their interplay. Sandhi: rajastama is rajaḥ+tamaḥ (-aḥ+t-→-as t-), with tamaḥ's own visarga then eliding before the following vowel i- of iti (as already at 13.1's kṣetrajña iti); dehinam avyayam is simply written joined, -m unaffected before the vowel.
#6
L: There, sattva, because-of-[its]-stainlessness illuminating, unafflicted, binds through attachment-to-happiness and through attachment-to-knowledge, O blameless one.
I: Of these, sattva, being stainless, is luminous and untainted; yet it binds through attachment to happiness and to knowledge, blameless one.
N: The first of the three definitions (continued at verses 7-8): sattva, nirmalatvāt, 'because of its stainlessness', is prakāśaka, 'illuminating' (a recurring image for sattva, echoed of brahman itself at 13.17), yet even sattva binds — through sukha-saṅga and jñāna-saṅga, 'attachment to happiness' and 'attachment to knowledge'. That a taste for knowledge itself can bind is a pointed warning, anticipated by verse 17's own sattvāt saṃjāyate jñānam. Sandhi: cānagha is ca+anagha (a+a→ā); nirmalatvāt prakāśakam anāmayam runs on as one fused token, its final -m before the actual next word's consonant p- unaffected.
#7
L: Rajas, of-the-nature-of-passion, know, arisen-from-craving-and-attachment; that binds, O Kaunteya, through attachment-to-action, the-embodied-one.
I: Know rajas to be passionate by nature, arising from craving and attachment; it binds the embodied soul, Kaunteya, through attachment to action.
N: The second definition: rajas is rāgātmakam, 'of the nature of passion', traced to tṛṣṇā and saṅga, 'craving' and 'attachment' — terms that recur through this chapter as the diagnostic vocabulary for what binds. Where sattva bound through happiness and knowledge, rajas binds karma-saṅgena, 'through attachment to action', restating in this chapter's own terms the teaching on niṣkāma karma of chapters 2-3. Sandhi: rāgātmakaṃ is rāga+ātmakam (a+ā→ā); tannibadhnāti is tat+nibadhnāti (-t+n-→-n n-).
#8
L: Tamas, but, born-of-ignorance, know, deluding of-all-embodied-beings; through heedlessness-laziness-and-sleep, that binds, O Bhārata.
I: But know tamas to be born of ignorance, the deluder of every embodied creature; it binds through heedlessness, laziness, and sleep, Bhārata.
N: The third definition completes the set: tamas is ajñānajam, 'born of ignorance' (contrasted with rajas's passion and sattva's stainless light), and mohanam, 'deluding'; its binding instruments are named as a compact triad, pramāda, ālasya, nidrā, 'heedlessness, laziness, sleep', whose negation (apramāda) will recur as a mark of the sattvic and the divine at 16.3. Sandhi: tamastv ajñānajaṃ packs tamaḥ+tu (-aḥ+t-→-as t-) and tu+ajñānajam (yaṇ sandhi, -u+a-→-v a-); pramādālasya- is pramāda+ālasya (a+ā→ā); nidrābhis tannibadhnāti packs nidrābhiḥ+tat (-iḥ+t-→-is t-) and tat+nibadhnāti (-t+n-→-n n-).
#9
L: Sattva attaches to-happiness, rajas to-action, O Bhārata; knowledge having-covered, but, tamas to-heedlessness attaches indeed.
I: Sattva attaches one to happiness, rajas to action, Bhārata; but tamas, covering over knowledge, attaches one instead to heedlessness.
N: This turns from defining each guṇa to how each is felt from within: each guṇa saṃjayati, 'attaches, binds', its subject to a characteristic state — sattva to sukha, rajas to karman, and tamas, having first āvṛtya, 'covered over', jñāna (an eclipse-like image that recurs at verse 17's tamaso bhavato'jñānam), to pramāda. Sandhi: jñānam āvṛtya is simply written joined, -m unaffected before the vowel; saṃjayaty uta is saṃjayati+uta (-i+u-→-y u-).
#10
L: Rajas-and-tamas having overcome, sattva prevails, O Bhārata; rajas sattva and-tamas-indeed, tamas sattva and-rajas likewise.
I: Sattva prevails, Bhārata, having overcome rajas and tamas; so too rajas prevails, overcoming sattva and tamas, and tamas, overcoming sattva and rajas.
N: This describes the guṇas' ceaseless rivalry (developed further at verses 11-13's symptoms of each guṇa's ascendancy): whichever is momentarily dominant does so by abhibhūya, 'having overcome', the other two. The second line is deliberately compressed, carrying over bhavati and abhibhūya from the first line by ellipsis into two further implied clauses — a terse listing typical of this chapter's more aphoristic verses. Sandhi: rajastamaścābhibhūya packs rajaḥ+tamaḥ (-aḥ+t-→-as t-), tamaḥ+ca (-aḥ+c-→-aś c-), and ca+abhibhūya (a+a→ā); tamaścaiva packs tamaḥ+ca (-aḥ+c-→-aś c-) and ca+eva (a+e→ai); rajastathā is rajaḥ+tathā (-aḥ+t-→-as t-).
#11
L: In-all-the-gates, in-this body, illumination arises; knowledge — when, then, one-should-know increased sattva, indeed.
I: When illumination arises at every gate of this body, then one should know that sattva has grown predominant.
N: This gives the diagnostic sign of sattva's ascendancy, paralleled for rajas and tamas at verses 12-13: sarva-dvāreṣu, 'at all the gates' (the senses, pictured as doorways of the body, as already at 5.13's sarva-dvāreṣu dehe), prakāśa arising is the mark that sattva has grown vivṛddham, 'increased, predominant'. Sandhi: dehe'sminprakāśa packs dehe+asmin (-e+a-→-e' with avagraha) and asmin+prakāśaḥ (simply joined before the consonant p-, prakāśaḥ's own visarga then eliding before the following vowel u- of upajāyate); vidyād vivṛddhaṃ is vidyāt+vivṛddham (-t+v-→-d v-); sattvam ity uta packs sattvam+iti (simply joined, -m unaffected before the vowel) and iti+uta (-i+u-→-y u-).
#12
L: Greed, activity, undertaking-of-actions, restlessness, longing — these arise, in-rajas, when increased, O bull-among-the-Bharatas.
I: Greed, engagement, the taking up of actions, restlessness, longing — these arise when rajas has grown predominant, bull among the Bharatas.
N: The symptoms of rajas's ascendancy, matching sattva's single sign at verse 11 with a fivefold list: lobha, 'greed'; pravṛtti, 'activity'; ārambha, 'undertaking [of action]'; aśama, 'restlessness'; spṛhā, 'longing' — the cluster of qualities driving restless action already diagnosed as rajas's danger in chapters 2-3. Sandhi: pravṛttir ārambhaḥ is pravṛttiḥ+ārambhaḥ (-iḥ+ā-→-ir ā-); rajasyetāni is rajasi+etāni (-i+e-→-y e-); vivṛddhe is a locative-absolute participle agreeing with an unexpressed rajasi, 'when [rajas] has increased' — the same construction recurs, with tamasi, at verse 13.
#13
L: Lack-of-illumination and inactivity, heedlessness, and delusion indeed — these arise, in-tamas, when increased, O joy-of-the-Kurus.
I: Lack of light, inertia, heedlessness, and delusion — these arise when tamas has grown predominant, joy of the Kurus.
N: The symptoms of tamas's ascendancy, in parallel with verses 11-12: aprakāśa, 'lack of illumination' (the negation of sattva's own mark from verse 11), apravṛtti, 'inactivity' (the negation of rajas's pravṛtti from verse 12), pramāda, 'heedlessness' (tamas's own binding-instrument, named already at verse 8), and moha, 'delusion'. Sandhi: aprakāśo'pravṛttiś ca packs aprakāśaḥ+apravṛttiḥ (-aḥ+a-→-o' with avagraha) and apravṛttiḥ+ca (-iḥ+c-→-iś c-); moha eva shows the visarga of mohaḥ eliding before the following vowel e-; tamasyetāni is tamasi+etāni (-i+e-→-y e-), matching verse 12's rajasyetāni.
#14
L: When in-sattva-increased, but, to-dissolution goes the-body-bearer, then to-the-worlds-of-those-who-know-the-highest, stainless, he attains.
I: But when the embodied one dies while sattva predominates, he attains to the stainless worlds of those who know the highest.
N: This opens the chapter's account of destiny after death, keyed to whichever guṇa predominates at the moment of dying (continued at verse 15 for rajas and tamas): deha-bhṛt, 'the body-bearer', dying sattve pravṛddhe, 'when sattva has increased' (a locative absolute), reaches uttama-vidāṃ lokān amalān, 'the stainless worlds of those who know the highest' — recasting, in the guṇas' own terms, the teaching on the paths after death already given at 8.23-26. Sandhi: tadottamavidāṃ is tadā+uttama-vidām (ā+u→o); lokān amalān and amalān pratipadyate are both simply written joined, within one long fused compound token.
#15
L: Having-gone to-dissolution in-rajas, among-those-attached-to-action he is born; likewise, one-dissolved in-tamas, in-wombs-of-the-deluded he is born.
I: One who dies while rajas predominates is born among those attached to action; and one who dies in tamas is born among the deluded.
N: This completes verses 14-15's threefold account of rebirth by guṇa: dying rajasi, 'in rajas', one is born karma-saṅgiṣu, 'among those attached to action' (a fittingly restless destiny for rajas's own besetting attachment, named already at verse 7); dying tamasi, 'in tamas', one is born mūḍha-yoniṣu, 'in wombs of the deluded' — the lowest of the three destinies, matching verse 18's ranking of the guṇas as high, middle, and low. Sandhi: pralīnas tamasi is pralīnaḥ+tamasi (-aḥ+t-→-as t-).
#16
L: Of-action, well-done, they say, of-sattva, stainless, [is] the-fruit; of-rajas, but, the-fruit [is] pain; ignorance [is] the-fruit of-tamas.
I: The fruit of a good action, they say, is sattva's own, and stainless; the fruit of rajas is suffering; the fruit of tamas is ignorance.
N: This states the fruit (phala) proper to each guṇa's characteristic action: sukṛta, 'good, well-done [action]', yields a phalam that is sāttvikam nirmalam, 'sattva-natured and stainless'; rajas's fruit is duḥkham, 'pain' (the cost of its restless activity, cf. 18.24's rājasa karma as bahv-āyāsam, 'much toil'); tamas's fruit is simply ajñānam, 'ignorance' — deeds done in delusion produce nothing but more delusion. Sandhi: sukṛtasyāhuḥ is sukṛtasya+āhuḥ (a+ā→ā); rajasastu is rajasaḥ+tu (-aḥ+t-→-as t-); duḥkham ajñānaṃ is simply written joined, -m unaffected before the vowel.
#17
L: From-sattva arises knowledge, from-rajas greed indeed, and; heedlessness-and-delusion from-tamas arise, and ignorance too, and.
I: From sattva arises knowledge, from rajas greed; from tamas arise heedlessness and delusion, and ignorance as well.
N: This names the psychological products of each guṇa, paralleling verse 16's fruits of action: sattva yields jñānam, 'knowledge' (though verse 6 has already warned that even attachment to this knowledge can bind); rajas yields lobha, 'greed' (echoing verse 12's lobhaḥ as rajas's first symptom); tamas yields pramāda-mohau, 'heedlessness and delusion' (again echoing verses 8 and 13), and ajñānam, 'ignorance', closing the list where tamas also began, since ignorance is both its origin (verse 8's ajñānajam) and its fruit. Sandhi: sattvātsaṃjāyate is simply written joined (both dental consonants, no change); rajaso is rajasaḥ, -aḥ before l-→-o; lobha eva shows the visarga of lobhaḥ eliding before the vowel e-; tamaso is tamasaḥ, -aḥ before bh-→-o; bhavato'jñānam eva packs bhavataḥ+ajñānam (-aḥ+a-→-o' with avagraha) and ajñānam+eva (simply joined, -m unaffected before the vowel).
#18
L: Upward go those-abiding-in-sattva; in-the-middle stand those-of-rajas; those-abiding-in-the-operation-of-the-lowest-guṇa go downward, those-of-tamas.
I: Those established in sattva rise upward; those of rajas remain in the middle; those abiding in the lowest guṇa's operation, the ones of tamas, sink downward.
N: This closes the chapter's account of the guṇas' effects with a ranked cosmology matching verses 14-15's account of rebirth: sattva-sthāḥ, 'those abiding in sattva', go ūrdhvam, 'upward'; rājasāḥ, 'those of rajas', remain madhye, 'in the middle'; and tāmasāḥ, 'those of tamas', described as jaghanya-guṇa-vṛtti-sthāḥ, 'abiding in the operation of the lowest guṇa' (jaghanya, 'last, lowest', marking tamas as bottom of the three), go adhaḥ, 'downward'. The vulgate text, followed here, reads jaghanya-guṇa-vṛtti-sthāḥ, with vṛtti, 'operation, function'; the BORI critical edition instead reads jaghanyaguṇavṛttasthāḥ, with vṛtta, 'turn, state, condition', in its place — 'situated in the state of the lowest guṇa' rather than 'in its operation' — a real vulgate/BORI variant, not a misprint, though the sense is barely affected either way. Sandhi: adho is adhaḥ, -aḥ before g-→-o.
#19
L: No other than-the-guṇas as-agent when the-seer perceives, and beyond-the-guṇas what he knows — he attains my-state-of-being.
I: When the seer perceives no agent other than the guṇas, and knows what lies beyond the guṇas, he attains to my own state of being.
N: This opens the chapter's third movement (verses 19-20), the promise of liberation through discernment: whoever, as draṣṭā, 'the seer', sees no kartāram anyaṃ guṇebhyaḥ, 'agent other than the guṇas' (i.e. recognizes that all action belongs to the guṇas' interplay, not to the self, as already taught at 3.27 and 13.29), and further vetti guṇebhyaḥ param, 'knows what is beyond the guṇas' (the untouched self), reaches mad-bhāvam, 'my own state of being' — the very promise already made in these terms at 13.18. Sandhi: nānyaṃ is na+anyam (a+a→ā); draṣṭānupaśyati is draṣṭā+anupaśyati (ā+a→ā); guṇebhyaśca is guṇebhyaḥ+ca (-aḥ+c-→-aś c-); so'dhigacchati is saḥ+adhigacchati (-aḥ+a-→-o' with avagraha).
#20
L: These three guṇas having transcended, the-embodied-one, arisen-from-the-body, from-birth-death-old-age-and-suffering freed, immortality attains.
I: Having transcended these three guṇas that arise from the body, the embodied soul is freed from birth, death, old age, and suffering, and attains immortality.
N: This closes the third movement with the chapter's central promise: the dehī, 'embodied one', having atītya, 'transcended', the trīn guṇān etān, 'these three guṇas' — themselves deha-samudbhavān, 'arising from the body' (from embodiment in nature, not from the true self) — becomes vimuktaḥ, 'freed', from janma-mṛtyu-jarā-duḥkhaiḥ, 'birth, death, old age, and suffering' (the standard fourfold formula for saṃsāra, echoing 13.8's janma-mṛtyu-jarā-vyādhi-duḥkha-doṣa-anudarśanam), and aśnute, 'attains', amṛtam, immortality — setting up Arjuna's question, in the next verse, about what such transcendence looks like from outside. Sandhi: guṇān etān atītya and trīn dehī each simply write a final nasal joined across the word-boundary; the fused second-line compound packs duḥkhaiḥ+vimuktaḥ (-aiḥ+v-→-air v-) and vimuktaḥ+amṛtam (-aḥ+a-→-o' with avagraha).
#21
L: By-what marks, these-three-guṇas-transcended, is-one, O Lord? What [is his] conduct, and how does-he-go-beyond these-three-guṇas?
I: By what marks, Lord, is one known who has gone beyond these three guṇas? What is his conduct, and how does he transcend them?
N: Arjuna's question, prompted directly by verse 20's promise, opens the chapter's final movement (verses 21-27): he asks for liṅgaiḥ, 'marks, signs' by which such a person could be recognized, ācāraḥ, '[his] conduct', and the manner (katham) of his transcendence — three questions Kṛṣṇa's answer (verses 22-26) addresses roughly in turn. Sandhi: kair liṅgais trīn guṇān etān atīto packs kaiḥ+liṅgaiḥ (-aiḥ+l-→-air l-), liṅgaiḥ+trīn (-aiḥ+t-→-ais t-), and atītaḥ+bhavati (-aḥ before bh-→-o); kim ācāraḥ is simply written joined; caitāṃstrīnguṇānativartate packs ca+etān (a+e→ai) and etān+trīn (-n+t-→-ṃs t-).
#22
L: Illumination, and activity, and delusion indeed, O Pāṇḍava — he hates-not [them] arisen, nor ceased desires.
I: One who neither hates illumination, activity, and delusion when they have arisen, nor desires them when they have ceased, Pāṇḍava —
N: Kṛṣṇa's answer begins here and runs through verse 25. Prakāśa, pravṛtti, and moha, 'illumination, activity, and delusion', name sattva's, rajas's, and tamas's characteristic effects already defined at verses 11-13; the guṇātīta neither dveṣṭi, 'hates', them saṃpravṛttāni, 'when they have arisen', nor kāṅkṣati, 'desires', them nivṛttāni, 'when they have ceased' — indifference to the guṇas' coming and going, not their suppression, is the mark Arjuna asked for. This clause has no subject of its own yet; it is completed by the relative yaḥ, 'who', that opens verse 23. Sandhi: mohameva is moham+eva, simply joined, -m unaffected before the vowel.
#23
L: As-if-indifferent seated, by-the-guṇas who is not moved; '[merely] the-guṇas operate' — thus, who abides, does-not-waver.
I: he sits as if indifferent, unmoved by the guṇas; who abides thinking only 'it is the guṇas that are operating', and does not waver —
N: This continues verse 22's description with the sentence's main relative clauses: udāsīna-vat āsīnaḥ, 'seated as if indifferent/neutral' (a memorable image of studied detachment), guṇaiḥ na vicālyate, 'not moved by the guṇas', and abiding in the settled understanding guṇāḥ vartante iti eva, '[it is] merely [that] the guṇas operate' — restating verse 19's own insight that the guṇas alone act — and so neṅgate, 'does not waver, stir'. Vartanta, the verb form used here, is a shortened epic ('chāndasa', Vedic-style) form of vartante before iti, already noted as such by Śaṅkara. Sandhi: guṇair yo is guṇaiḥ+yaḥ (-aiḥ+y-→-air y-); ity eva is iti+eva (-i+e-→-y e-); yo'vatiṣṭhati is yaḥ+avatiṣṭhati (-aḥ+a-→-o' with avagraha); neṅgate is na+iṅgate (a+i→e).
#24
L: Equal-in-pain-and-pleasure, self-abiding, regarding-clod-stone-and-gold-as-equal, equal-toward-the-pleasant-and-unpleasant, steady, equal-to-blame-and-self-praise —
I: equal in pain and pleasure, self-possessed, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold alike; equal toward the pleasant and unpleasant, steady, equal to blame and to praise of himself —
N: The description continues with a run of compounds naming the guṇātīta's equanimity toward every ordinary pair of opposites — pain and pleasure, a clod of earth, a stone, and gold treated alike, the pleasant and the unpleasant, blame and self-praise — generalizing the equanimity already commended at 2.38 and 12.18-19. Svastha, 'self-abiding, self-possessed' (literally 'standing in oneself'), names the ground of this equanimity: rooted in the self, not in the guṇas' fluctuations. Sandhi: loṣṭāśma- is loṣṭa+aśma (a+a→ā); priyāpriyo is priya+apriya (a+a→ā), with the compound's own -aḥ before dh-→-o; nindātma- is nindā+ātma (ā+ā→ā).
#25
L: Equal in-honor-and-dishonor, equal toward-the-sides-of-friend-and-foe, one-who-has-abandoned-all-undertakings — gone-beyond-the-guṇas, he, is called.
I: equal in honor and dishonor, equal toward the side of friend and of foe alike, having given up every undertaking — such a one is said to have gone beyond the guṇas.
N: This completes the description of the guṇātīta begun at verse 22: equal to māna and apamāna, 'honor and dishonor', and to mitra and ari, 'friend and foe', he is sarva-ārambha-parityāgī, 'one who has abandoned every undertaking' (not inaction as such, but freedom from the driven initiative that is rajas's own mark at verse 12's ārambhaḥ) — guṇa-atītaḥ, 'gone beyond the guṇas', exactly the state Arjuna asked about at verse 21. The vulgate reading, followed here, is māna-apamānayoḥ, 'of honor and dishonor'; the BORI critical edition reads mānāvamānayoḥ instead, with avamāna (a near-synonym of apamāna, both meaning 'disrespect, dishonor') in its place — a real vulgate/BORI variant, not a misprint, and not a difference of sense. Sandhi: mānāpamānayoḥ is māna+apamānayoḥ (a+a→ā), the whole compound's own -oḥ+t-→-os t- before the first tulyaḥ, whose own -aḥ+t-→-as t- precedes the second tulyaḥ, whose own -aḥ before m-→-o; sarvārambha- is sarva+ārambha (a+ā→ā); guṇātītaḥ is guṇa+atīta (a+a→ā).
#26
L: And who me with-unwavering-devotion, with-the-yoga-of-devotion, serves — he, these-guṇas having-fully-transcended, for-the-state-of-being-brahman becomes fit.
I: And whoever serves me with unwavering devotion, through the yoga of devotion, transcends these guṇas entirely and becomes fit for the state of being brahman.
N: This closes the description of the guṇātīta by adding what the preceding, more austere account (verses 22-25) has not yet mentioned: bhakti, devotion. One who sevate, 'serves', Kṛṣṇa avyabhicāreṇa bhakti-yogena, 'with unwavering devotion, through the yoga of devotion' (the same insistence on undivided constancy as 12.6's ananyena eva yogena and 13.10's ananya-yogena), and samatītya, 'having fully transcended', the guṇas, becomes fit brahma-bhūyāya, 'for the state of being brahman' — the same term, brahma-bhūya, that names the culmination of the whole poem's teaching at 18.53, here reached through devotion rather than the discernment of verses 19-23 alone. Sandhi: yo'vyabhicāreṇa is yaḥ+avyabhicāreṇa (-aḥ+a-→-o' with avagraha); guṇānsamatītyaitān packs guṇān+samatītya (simply joined before the consonant s-) and samatītya+etān (a+e→ai), running on, still joined, into brahmabhūyāya.
#27
L: Of-brahman, for, [I am] the-foundation, I, of-the-immortal and of-the-imperishable, and; of-the-eternal and of-dharma, of-absolute-happiness, and.
I: For I am the foundation of brahman — of the immortal and the imperishable, of the eternal dharma, and of unmixed happiness.
N: The chapter closes with Kṛṣṇa's own self-declaration as pratiṣṭhā, 'foundation, resting-place', of brahman itself — a striking claim that reverses the more usual direction of chapters 13-14 (where brahman has stood as the ultimate ground, e.g. 13.12-17, and Kṛṣṇa's relation to it stated more modestly at 13.12's mat-param) by making Kṛṣṇa the support of brahman, of amṛta and avyaya, 'the immortal and the imperishable', of śāśvata dharma (dharma kept untranslated per convention), and of sukham aikāntikam, 'unmixed, absolute happiness' — four genitives in apposition gathering everything ultimate the poem has so far named, all grounded, this verse claims, in Kṛṣṇa himself. It closes the chapter on a note that prepares the still bolder claims about Kṛṣṇa's relation to every being and every path made in chapter 18. Sandhi: pratiṣṭhāhaṃ is pratiṣṭhā+aham (ā+a→ā); ahamamṛtasyāvyayasya packs aham+amṛtasya (simply joined before the vowel) and amṛtasya+avyayasya (a+a→ā); sukhasyaikāntikasya is sukhasya+aikāntikasya (a+ai→ai).
